I am 62 years old and farming alone on these 10.1 mu, so I must be honest about what my back and my two hands can handle after 40 years in the fields. Cotton is my foundation — it has fed me for decades and I know its temperament in Quzhou soil like I know my own palm. I plant improved Bt cotton seed across the whole farm because the bollworm pressure here is real and I do not have young labor to spray every week. In early April I will rotary till once to warm and loosen the soil, then put down about 16 jin equivalent of nitrogen, 6 of phosphorus, and 5 of potassium per mu as base and side-dressing. My well gives reliable water, so I will irrigate four times: at seedling establishment, early flowering, peak boll-setting, and when the bolls begin to crack. Four pesticide sprays should suffice with the Bt variety.

On 2.5 mu of the wider cotton rows I will intercrop hybrid chili in spring — the cash return at the Quzhou market is too good to ignore, but I limit it to 2.5 mu because hand-picking chili every few days in autumn will bend my waist to the ground. Chili is greedy for potassium and water, so I will give it roughly 14-5-12 NPK per mu and irrigate five times. 

For mungbean, I will relay-plant 1 mu into standing cotton in early June with no-tillage — just dibble the seed into the row middles. Mungbean fixes its own nitrogen, so I only top-dress a little phosphorus and potassium, about 3 and 2 per mu. It will catch two irrigations from the cotton schedule and needs only two pesticide sprays for pod borer. By September I can harvest the pods without much bending, and the leftover roots will leave some nitrogen in the soil for next year’s cotton. I have done this layout before; it is not greedy for labor, and at my age that matters more than ambition.
